BLE-01.brief: The board's custom service is full of characteristics. Start by simply looking.

BLE-02.brief: This value is readable, but not in a form you would want to submit.

BLE-03.brief: One characteristic refuses to be read. It has other ways of talking.

BLE-04.brief: The flag arrives in pieces, and the board wants to know you got each one.

BLE-05.brief: A sealed hatch and a panel next to it. The panel tells you what it wants.

BLE-06.brief: A characteristic so boring nobody looks twice at it.

BLE-07.brief: You don't always need to connect to learn something.

BLE-08.brief: A long telemetry value. Is your client showing you all of it?

BLE-09.brief: A locker that only opens for a properly paired client.

BLE-10.brief: A four-digit keypad that does not like being rushed. Needs scripting.

BLE-11.brief: A sequencer that wants a short pattern, in order, and quickly. Needs scripting.

BTC-01.brief: The board offers a serial-style console over Bluetooth Classic. Get a terminal on it.
tools: picocom / tio on an RFCOMM tty (rfcomm is legacy)

BTC-02.brief: The console's help is helpful, but not complete.

BTC-03.brief: The board says more about itself than its name before you ever connect.

CRY-01.brief: An old-school cipher, and a key that is scattered across the CTF. You will need to visit other tracks.

CRY-02.brief: An encryption oracle that will happily encrypt whatever you give it, along with something you want. Needs scripting.

CRY-03.brief: Two encrypted messages. One of them you can already guess.

HW-01.brief: The board checks something about its own pins when it starts. Skip this one if you don't have a jumper wire.

HW-02.brief: The onboard LED is trying to tell you something.

HW-03.brief: A pin is toggling at a frequency unique to your board. The answer is a number (answer HW-03 <value>). Skip this one if you don't have a logic analyzer.

HW-04.brief: The board talks on an I2C bus to a device that isn't there. Skip this one if you don't have a logic analyzer.

HW-05.brief: Something is being sent over SPI every few seconds. Skip this one if you don't have a logic analyzer.

HW-06.brief: Four bare pins are a keypad. You need the code. Don't touch the pads while the board boots.

RE-01.brief: Not everything in flash is code.

RE-02.brief: The firmware keeps a few things in its key-value store, and one of them is not quite in the clear.

RE-03.brief: The console has an unlock command. You don't have the key.

RE-04.brief: There is a binary blob in the board's filesystem. It isn't readable as is.

SER-01.brief: The board says a lot when it boots. Did you read all of it?

SER-02.brief: The board has a second serial port that nobody connected. Skip this one if you have neither a 3.3 V USB-UART adapter nor a logic analyzer (an analyzer on GPIO17 plus GND, with sigrok's UART decoder, works too). UART2 pins: board TX = GPIO17, board RX = GPIO16; connect GND too.

SER-03.brief: A debug login with a per-board password. Guessing by hand is hopeless. Needs scripting.

SER-04.brief: Some consoles hide a back door behind the right keys.

WEB-01.brief: The board runs its own access point. You won't find it in your network list.

WEB-02.brief: What a browser shows you is not everything the server sent.

WEB-03.brief: There is an admin area. You are not an admin. Yet.

WEB-04.brief: An API that is picky about who it talks to.

WEB-05.brief: You can log in as a guest. The session token decides what you are.

WEB-06.brief: A diagnostics page for reading log files. Only log files, surely.

WEB-07.brief: A chatty WebSocket. Most of it is noise.

WEB-08.brief: Not every service on the board is linked from its web pages.

WEB-09.brief: A door that is closed until you knock the right way. The console has something to say about it.
